topic: Flow basics: cold flows, operators & flowOn

questions.question: Assigning `val f = flow { ... }` to a variable runs the builder block immediately, and later collectors receive the values it produced.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A `flow { }` is cold: building it only stores the block. The block runs from the start for each terminal operator, separately for every collector. Nothing is produced or cached at creation time.

questions.explanation: Nothing runs when the flow is built, so built prints first. Each terminal operator re-runs the block, so start prints twice. `first()` takes the first value and then cancels the flow, so the second run prints only 1.

questions.question: Right after this line runs, how many times has the body of the upstream `repo.items()` flow executed?
options: 0: map and filter just build a new flow
1: map starts collecting the upstream flow
2: each operator collects the upstream once
1: filter is the terminal operator here
questions.explanation: `map` and `filter` are intermediate operators: they wrap the upstream and return another cold `Flow` without collecting anything. Work starts only when a terminal operator like `collect`, `first` or `toList` is called. Neither of these operators is terminal.

questions.explanation: A flow pushes each value through the whole chain before the next one is emitted, unlike a List where each operator finishes the whole collection first. So each value goes through map, then filter, then collect. The value 2 (from 1 * 2) fails `it > 2`, so there is no got 2.

questions.question: This is collected from a coroutine on `Dispatchers.Main`. Which steps run on `Dispatchers.IO`?
questions.code:
flow { emit(load()) }      // A
    .map { parse(it) }     // B
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)
    .map { format(it) }    // C
    .collect { show(it) }  // D
options: A and B on IO; C and D in the collector's context
Only A on IO; B, C and D run in the collector's context
A, B, C and D all run on IO once flowOn is applied
C and D on IO; A and B in the collector's context
questions.explanation: `flowOn` changes the context only of the operators above it (upstream); everything below it, including `collect`, stays in the collector's context. So the emitting block and the first `map` move to IO, while the second `map` and `collect` stay on Main. This is how flows keep context preservation: a flow can never change the collector's context.

questions.question: What happens when this flow is collected?
options: It throws IllegalStateException, since emitting from another context breaks the flow
It works, and the collector's lambda receives the value while running on Dispatchers.IO
It fails to compile because emit cannot be called from inside a withContext block
It deadlocks, since the collector waits on Main while emit waits on an IO thread
questions.explanation: The `flow { }` builder checks that `emit` is called from the same coroutine context as the collector; emitting inside `withContext` breaks that and throws `IllegalStateException` ("Flow invariant is violated"). The code compiles because the `FlowCollector` receiver is in scope inside the lambda. The fix is to drop `withContext` and add `.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)`.

questions.question: Which statements about the `catch` flow operator are true? Select all that apply.
options: It catches exceptions thrown by operators placed above it
It does not catch an exception thrown inside the final `collect { }` block
It can call `emit` to send a fallback value downstream
It also catches exceptions from operators placed below it
After catching, the upstream flow resumes from its next value
questions.explanation: `catch` only sees upstream exceptions, so failures in later operators or in `collect` pass through it; for those, move the work into `onEach` before `catch`. Inside `catch` you can `emit` a fallback or rethrow. The upstream has already completed with the error, so it does not resume; use `retry` if you want to re-run it.

questions.question: Why does the flow documentation treat this pattern as a bug?
options: emit runs downstream code, so the try also catches the collector's IOExceptions
emit is not a suspending call, so the try block can never catch an exception thrown by the upstream
A flow may only emit once per builder call, so the emit(-1) in the catch block throws immediately
Catch blocks inside flow { } run on another dispatcher, so emit(-1) breaks context preservation
questions.explanation: `emit` calls straight into the downstream operators and collector, so a `try` around it also catches exceptions that belong to the consumer. Swallowing them and emitting again breaks exception transparency, and the flow throws `IllegalStateException` on that later emit. Use the `catch` operator, which only handles upstream failures.

questions.question: A flow is collected with `.take(2)`. What happens to the upstream `flow { }` block right after the second value is delivered?
options: It's cancelled by an internal exception thrown from emit, so its finally blocks still run
It keeps running to completion, and take simply drops every value after the second one
It stays suspended forever at the third emit, since no collector ever asks for more values
It's moved into GlobalScope and finishes in the background without blocking the collector
questions.explanation: `take` stops the upstream by throwing an internal `AbortFlowException` out of the next `emit`, which unwinds the producer like a cancellation. Any `finally` or `onCompletion` cleanup in the upstream still runs, and the abort is caught inside `take`, so the collector completes normally. The producer is never left running or suspended.

questions.question: Inside a `flow { }` builder you may call `emit` from several `launch`ed child coroutines (for example inside `coroutineScope { }`) to produce values concurrently.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: `flow { }` is sequential and not thread-safe: emitting from another coroutine breaks context preservation and throws `IllegalStateException`. For concurrent producers use `channelFlow { }` (or `callbackFlow`), where children call `send` on a channel that is safe to share.
